title: AND, OR, NOT from Zero
goal: Tell propositions from non-propositions, use `¬ ∧ ∨` and their truth tables, know what a well-formed formula is, and read formulas aloud.
magic: Proposition = a claim that is T or F (even if nobody knows which).
Propositional logic only handles truth-functional joiners.
`∧`: both. `∨`: at least one (both is fine). `¬`: flip. "but" = `∧`.
`¬` binds first, then `∧ ∨` (always bracket a mix), then `⇒ ⇔`.
Read a formula from its main joiner.

blocks.title: 💡 Learn it, one idea at a time
Propositions: sentences that are true or false
blocks.summary: A proposition is a declarative sentence: it makes a claim that is either true or false.
blocks.picture: "The fridge is empty" can be checked: open the fridge. "Close the fridge!" can't be true or false; it's an order. Logic only works with the checkable kind.
blocks.official: A sentence is **declarative**, or a **proposition**, if it can meaningfully be said to be either **true or false** (Week 1, slide 51). We don't have to *know* which: "`xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ` has no non-trivial integer solutions for `n > 2`" is a proposition. **Not** propositions: nonsense, commands, questions, requests (slide 52).

watch.q: Which of these are propositions? (a) "Sydney is the capital of Australia." (b) "Is the build green?" (c) "Every even number above 2 is a sum of two primes." (d) "Please merge my PR."
steps: (a) A claim you can check. It's false (Canberra is), but false is fine: **proposition**.
(c) A claim. Nobody knows yet whether it's true (Goldbach's conjecture), but it is true or false: **proposition**.

tries.q: "Kafka stores messages in partitions." Proposition?
tries.why: It makes a checkable claim.

tries.q: "Restart the server now!" Proposition?
tries.why: It's a command. It can be obeyed or not, but not true or false.

tries.q: "There are infinitely many prime pairs like 11 and 13." Proposition?
tries.why: It's either true or false, even though no one knows which yet (the twin prime conjecture).

tries.q: "Flibber the snorkwhack." Proposition?
tries.why: It's not meaningful, so it can't be true or false.

trap.tempting: If nobody knows whether it's true, it isn't a proposition.
trap.correct: It only has to be **either** true or false. Unknown is fine; meaningless, commands and questions are not.
trap.test: Ask: could a perfect judge label it T or F? If yes, it's a proposition.

blocks.magic: Proposition = a claim that is either T or F (even if we don't know which).

blocks.title: Truth-functional joiners only
blocks.summary: Propositional logic handles joiners where the truth of the whole depends only on the truth of the parts.
blocks.picture: "It's raining and it's cold": if you know whether each part is true, you know the whole. "I stayed home **because** it rained": both parts can be true while the reason is false. Knowing the parts isn't enough.
blocks.official: Propositional logic represents constructions where the truth value of the compound sentence is **determined by the truth values of its parts** (Week 1, slide 53: *and*, *either … or*, *it is not the case that*). **Not** truth-functional: *believes that*, *because*, *after* (slide 54). Modal logics handle those.

watch.q: Is "The deploy failed after the tests passed" truth-functional?
steps: Suppose both parts are true: the deploy failed, and the tests passed.
The whole sentence could still be false (maybe the deploy failed *before* the tests ran).
So the parts' truth values don't fix the whole.
watch.answer: **Not truth-functional.** "After" adds timing, which `∧` can't express.

tries.q: "The cache is warm or the database is fast." Truth-functional?
tries.why: It's `c ∨ d`: knowing `c` and `d` settles it.

tries.q: "Priya knows that the release is on Friday." Truth-functional?
tries.why: The release can be on Friday while Priya doesn't know it. *Knows that* isn't determined by the part's truth.

tries.q: "It is not the case that every test passed." Truth-functional?
tries.why: It's `¬t`: flip the truth value of the part.

trap.tempting: Any sentence with two parts can be written with `∧`.
trap.correct: Only if the whole is fixed by the parts' truth values. *Because*, *after*, *believes* aren't.
trap.test: Make both parts true. Could the whole sentence still be false? Then it isn't truth-functional.

blocks.magic: Truth-functional = the parts' T/F decide the whole.

blocks.title: NOT, AND, OR and their English words
blocks.summary: `¬` flips. `∧` needs both. `∨` needs at least one. "but" is `∧`, and "or" includes both.
blocks.picture: A burger order: "cheese AND bacon" means you get both. "Cheese OR bacon" means at least one, and both is fine. "NOT onions" means the opposite of onions.
blocks.official: Week 1, slide 55: `∧` for "and", "but", ";", ":" · `∨` for "or", "either … or …" · `¬` for "not", "it is not the case that". Tables: `A ∧ B` is T only when both are T. `A ∨ B` is F only when both are F. `¬A` flips `A`.

watch.q: Translate "The API is slow, but it isn't down." (`s` = the API is slow, `d` = it is down)
steps: "but" joins two claims that are both true: `∧`.
watch.answer: **`s ∧ ¬d`**. "But" sounds like a contrast, but logically it's just AND.

tries.q: Translate "Either the queue is full or the consumer is down." (`q`, `c`)
tries.why: "Either … or" is still inclusive `∨` in the slides (both may be true).
tries.letters: `q` = the queue is full · `c` = the consumer is down

tries.q: Translate "It is not the case that the build passed." (`b`)
tries.why: "It is not the case that" is `¬` in front of the whole claim.

tries.q: Translate "The disk is full; the logs stopped." (`f`, `l`)
tries.why: A semicolon joining two claims is `∧` (slide 55).

tries.q: Value of `¬a ∨ b` when `a = T, b = F`?
tries.why: `¬a` = F and `b` = F. `∨` of two Fs is F.

tries.q: Value of `a ∧ ¬(b ∨ c)` when `a = T, b = F, c = F`?
tries.why: `b ∨ c` = F, so `¬(b ∨ c)` = T. T ∧ T = T.

trap.tempting: "or" means one or the other but not both.
trap.correct: In logic, `∨` is **inclusive**: both true makes `A ∨ B` true. "Exactly one" is a different joiner, `⊕`.
trap.test: Check the row where both are T: `∨` gives T.

blocks.magic: `∧`: both. `∨`: at least one (both is fine). `¬`: flip. "but" = `∧`.

blocks.title: What counts as a formula (and how brackets work)
blocks.summary: Formulas are built by one small set of rules. Anything else, like `p ¬ q`, isn't a formula.
blocks.picture: Like a programming language's grammar: `(a && b)` compiles, `a && && b` doesn't. Logic formulas have a grammar too.
blocks.official: Week 1, slide 63: `⊤`, `⊥` and every letter are formulas. If `φ` is a formula, so is `¬φ`. If `φ`, `ψ` are formulas, so are `(φ ∧ ψ)`, `(φ ∨ ψ)`, `(φ ⇒ ψ)`, `(φ ⇔ ψ)`. Nothing else. `⊤` is always true, `⊥` always false. **Convention:** drop brackets when there's no ambiguity. `¬` binds tightest, then `∧` and `∨`, then `⇒` and `⇔`. The slides don't rank `∧` against `∨`, so always bracket a mix.

watch.q: Is `¬(p ∧ ⊤) ⇒ ¬¬q` a formula? Where do the brackets go?
steps: `¬(p ∧ ⊤)` is a formula. `¬q`, then `¬¬q` are formulas.
Joining them with `⇒` gives a formula. `¬` binds tighter than `⇒`, so no extra brackets are needed.

tries.q: Is `p ∧ ∨ q` a formula?
tries.why: `∧` needs a formula on each side, and `∨ q` isn't one.

tries.q: Is `¬¬¬⊥` a formula?
tries.why: `⊥` is a formula, and `¬` can be applied again and again.

tries.q: Add the brackets the convention hides: `¬a ∧ b ⇒ c`.
tries.why: `¬` grabs `a` first, then `∧` joins `¬a` and `b`, then `⇒` is last.

tries.q: Why must `p ∧ q ∨ r` be bracketed in this course?
tries.a: Because the slides don't say whether `∧` or `∨` binds tighter, so it could mean `(p ∧ q) ∨ r` or `p ∧ (q ∨ r)`, and those differ.
tries.why: Row `p = F, r = T`: the first is T, the second is F.

trap.correct: `¬` binds tightest: `¬p ∧ q` = `(¬p) ∧ q`. For "not both", you must write `¬(p ∧ q)`.
trap.test: Row `p = F, q = F`: `(¬p) ∧ q` = F but `¬(p ∧ q)` = T. Different.

blocks.title: Reading a formula back into English
blocks.summary: Find the main joiner first; it becomes the backbone of the English sentence.
blocks.picture: Reading a formula is like reading code: find the outermost `if`, and the rest hangs off it.
blocks.official: Put the brackets back using the binding rules, find the **main joiner** (the one applied last), and read it first: `⇒` → "if … then …", `⇔` → "… if and only if …", `∧` → "… and …", `∨` → "… or …", `¬` → "not / it is not the case that".

watch.q: With `c` = it's cold, `h` = the heater is on, `w` = a window is open: read `¬c ∨ h ⇒ ¬w`.
steps: Main joiner: `⇒`, so the sentence is "If …, then …".
Left part: "it isn't cold or the heater is on". Right: "no window is open".
watch.answer: "**If it isn't cold or the heater is on, then no window is open.**"

tries.q: With `r` = it rains, `b` = I bike, `t` = I take the train: read `r ⇒ ¬b ∧ t`.
tries.a: "If it rains, then I don't bike and I take the train."
tries.why: Brackets: `r ⇒ (¬b ∧ t)`. Main joiner `⇒`.

tries.q: Same letters: read `¬(r ∧ b)`.
tries.a: "It's not the case that it rains and I bike", i.e. "I don't bike in the rain".
tries.why: Main joiner `¬`, applied to the whole bracket.

tries.q: Same letters: read `t ⇔ r ∨ ¬b`.
tries.a: "I take the train if and only if it rains or I don't bike."
tries.why: Brackets: `t ⇔ (r ∨ ¬b)`. `⇔` is the main joiner.

tries.q: Same letters: read `(b ⇒ ¬r) ⇒ t`.
tries.a: "If (I bike only when it isn't raining), then I take the train." Or: "If biking means no rain, then I take the train."
tries.why: The main joiner is the **second** `⇒`; the bracket is its condition.

trap.tempting: Read left to right, word for word.
trap.correct: Find the main joiner first. `¬c ∨ h ⇒ ¬w` starts with "If", not with "Not".
trap.test: Put all brackets back, then read the outermost joiner first.

blocks.magic: Brackets back → main joiner first → read the pieces.

blocks.title: Simplifying `if` conditions
blocks.summary: Turn a code condition into letters, simplify the formula, turn it back into shorter code.
blocks.picture: A code reviewer spots `if (x > 0 || (x <= 0 && y > 100))` and says "that's just `x > 0 || y > 100`". Logic proves the reviewer is right.
blocks.official: Week 1, slide 56: with `p` = `(x > 0)` and `q` = `(y > 100)`, the condition `x > 0 or (x <= 0 and y > 100)` is `p ∨ (¬p ∧ q)`. Its truth table matches `p ∨ q`, so the code can be simplified to `if x > 0 or y > 100`. Note `x <= 0` is exactly `¬p`.

watch.q: Simplify `if ready and not (ready and failed):`

tries.q: Simplify `if not (not a or not b):`
tries.why: De Morgan + double negation: `¬(¬a ∨ ¬b)` = `a ∧ b`.

tries.q: Simplify `if cached or (not cached and fresh):`
tries.why: Same shape as the lecture example: `c ∨ (¬c ∧ f)` = `c ∨ f`.

tries.q: Simplify `if admin or (admin and owner):`
tries.why: `a ∨ (a ∧ o)` = `a`: if `a` is false, the bracket is false too.

trap.tempting: Only a compiler can tell that two conditions are the same.
trap.correct: A truth table over the letters proves it for every input, once the comparisons are replaced by letters.
trap.test: Replace each comparison by a letter; check that opposite comparisons (`x > 0`, `x <= 0`) become `p` and `¬p`.

blocks.magic: Comparisons → letters → simplify → back to code.

items.q: "Tomorrow is Friday." Proposition?
items.why: It's either true or false.

items.q: "Why is the build red?" Proposition?
items.why: It's a question.

items.q: Value of `T ∧ F`?
items.why: `∧` needs both.

items.q: Value of `F ∨ T`?
items.why: `∨` needs at least one.

items.q: Value of `¬(T ∨ T)`?
items.why: T ∨ T = T; flip it: F.

items.q: Translate "The tests pass and the linter is happy." (`t`, `l`)
items.why: "and" is `∧`.

items.q: Translate "The coffee is hot but not strong." (`h`, `s`)
items.why: "but" = `∧`; "not strong" = `¬s`.

items.q: Translate "It is not the case that the fan and the heater are both on." (`f`, `h`)
items.why: "It is not the case that" covers the whole "both" claim, so the `¬` goes outside a bracket.

items.q: Is "The server crashed because the disk was full" truth-functional?
items.why: Both parts can be true while the disk wasn't the cause.

items.q: Add the hidden brackets: `¬p ∨ q ⇔ r`.
items.why: `¬` first, then `∨`, then `⇔`.

items.q: Is `(p ⇒)` a formula?
items.why: `⇒` needs a formula on the right.

items.q: Evaluate `(a ∨ b) ∧ ¬(a ∧ b)` for all four rows (FF, FT, TF, TT).
items.why: It's T exactly when one of them is true: it's the "exactly one" joiner `⊕`.

blocks.sub: Problem set 2, Q1(b) style: describe formulas in English. Original letters and sentences.

items.q: `s` = the shop is open · `d` = it's a holiday · `m` = I buy milk. Describe `s ∧ ¬d ⇒ m` in English.
items.a: "If the shop is open and it isn't a holiday, then I buy milk."
items.why: Brackets: `(s ∧ ¬d) ⇒ m`. The main joiner is `⇒`.

items.q: Same letters. Describe `¬m ⇔ d ∨ ¬s` in English.
items.a: "I don't buy milk if and only if it's a holiday or the shop is closed."
items.why: Brackets: `¬m ⇔ (d ∨ ¬s)`. The main joiner is `⇔`.

items.q: Same letters. Describe `(d ⇒ ¬s) ∧ m` in English.
items.a: "The shop is closed whenever it's a holiday, and I buy milk."
items.why: The main joiner is `∧`: two separate claims.

items.q: Same letters. Describe `s ⇒ (d ⇒ ¬m)` in English.
items.a: "If the shop is open, then if it's a holiday I don't buy milk." Or: "When the shop is open on a holiday, I don't buy milk."
items.why: `A ⇒ (B ⇒ C)` reads as "if A and B, then C".

items.q: Which options are well-formed formulas (brackets may be dropped by convention)?
items.why: (2) has `∧` with nothing on the right. (5) puts `¬` after a letter, which the rules never allow.
items.nocheck: Well-formedness is a grammar question, not a truth-table one.

items.q: `x > 5` is `p` and `y = 0` is `q`. Simplify `if not (x <= 5 or y != 0) or (x > 5 and y != 0):`
Why does the slide say "Trump believes that Iran is developing nukes" is not truth-functional?
items.a: Its truth depends on what the person believes, not on whether the inner claim is true. The inner claim can be false while the belief exists, and vice versa.
items.why: "believes that" is a modal construction; modal logics extend propositional logic to handle it (slide 54).

items.q: Using the symbols `¬ p ∧ q` in exactly that order, and adding brackets however you like, how many formulas with **different meanings** can you make?
items.why: The only choice is what the `¬` covers: just `p`, or the whole `p ∧ q`. Row `p = F, q = F` tells them apart.

items.q: Is `(p ∨ q) ∧ r` the same as `p ∨ (q ∧ r)`? If not, give a row.
items.a: **No.** Row `p = T, r = F`: first F, second T.
items.why: This is why a mix of `∧` and `∨` always needs brackets.

items.q: Translate "It is not the case that the build and the deploy both failed, but the alerts fired." (`b`, `d`, `a`)
items.why: "but" = `∧` at the top. The `¬` covers only the "both failed" part.

items.q: "Delete the branch." Proposition?
Value of `¬F ∧ (F ∨ T)`?
Add brackets: `¬a ⇒ b ∧ c`.
Simplify `if x or (not x and y):`

lines: Propositions: declarative, T or F. Not: questions, commands, requests, nonsense.
Truth-functional: the parts' values decide the whole. *because, after, believes* are not.
`∧` = and / but / ; / :  ·  `∨` = or, either…or (inclusive)  ·  `¬` = not, it is not the case that.
Formula rules: letters, `⊤`, `⊥`; `¬φ`; `(φ ∧ ψ)`, `(φ ∨ ψ)`, `(φ ⇒ ψ)`, `(φ ⇔ ψ)`.
